{{Short description|Form of scientific experiment}}

A '''cluster-randomised controlled trial''' (cRCT, CRCT) is a type of [[randomised controlled trial]] in which groups of subjects (as opposed to individual subjects) are randomised.<ref name="Bland-2004">{{Cite journal | author = Bland JM | title = Cluster randomised trials in the medical literature: two bibliometric surveys | journal = BMC Med Res Methodol | volume = 4 | pages = 21 | year = 2004 | doi = 10.1186/1471-2288-4-21 | pmid = 15310402 | pmc=515302 | doi-access = free }}</ref> Cluster randomised controlled trials are also known as '''cluster-randomised trials''',<ref name="Campbell-2004">{{Cite journal | vauthors = Campbell MK, Elbourne DR, Altman DG, ((CONSORT group)) | title = CONSORT statement: extension to cluster randomised trials | journal = BMJ | volume = 328 | issue = 7441 | pages = 702–8 | year = 2004 | doi = 10.1136/bmj.328.7441.702 | url= | pmid = 15031246 | pmc=381234}}</ref> '''group-randomised trials''',<ref name="Murray-2004">{{Cite journal | vauthors = Murray DM, Varnell SP, Blitstein JL | title = Design and analysis of group-randomized trials: a review of recent methodological developments | journal = Am J Public Health | volume = 94 | issue = 3 | pages = 423–32 | year = 2004 | doi = 10.2105/AJPH.94.3.423 | pmid = 14998806 | pmc=1448268}}</ref><ref name="Patton-2006">{{Cite journal | vauthors = Patton GC, Bond L, Carlin JB, Thomas L, Butler H, Glover S, Catalano R, Bowes G | title = Promoting social inclusion in schools: a group-randomized trial of effects on student health risk behavior and well-being | journal = Am J Public Health | volume = 96 | issue = 9 | pages = 1582–7 | year = 2006 | doi = 10.2105/AJPH.2004.047399 | pmid = 16873760 | pmc=1551970}}</ref> and '''place-randomized trials'''.<ref name="Boruch-2004">{{Cite journal | authorlink1 = Robert F. Boruch | vauthors = Boruch R, May H, Turner H, Lavenberg J, Petrosino A, De Moya D, Grimshaw J, Foley E | title = Estimating the effects of interventions that are deployed in many places: place-randomized trials | journal = [[American Behavioral Scientist]] | volume = 47 | issue = 5 | pages = 608–633 | year = 2004 | doi = 10.1177/0002764203259291 | s2cid = 910678 | url = http://spabs.highwire.org/cgi/content/abstract/47/5/608 | url-access = subscription }}{{Dead link|date=July 2019 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> Cluster-randomised controlled trials are used when there is a strong reason for randomising treatment and control groups over randomising participants.<ref name="Murray">{{cite journal|doi=10.1146/annurev-publhealth-040119-094027|title=Essential Ingredients and Innovations in the Design and Analysis of Group-Randomized Trials|year=2020|last1=Murray|first1=David M.|last2=Taljaard|first2=Monica|last3=Turner|first3=Elizabeth L.|last4=George|first4=Stephanie M.|journal=Annual Review of Public Health|volume=41|pages=1–19|pmid=31869281|doi-access=free}}</ref>

==Prevalence==

A 2004 [[Bibliometrics|bibliometric]] study documented an increasing number of publications in the medical literature on cluster-randomised controlled trials since the 1980s.<ref name="Bland-2004"/> 

==Advantages==
Advantages of cluster-randomised controlled trials over individually randomised controlled trials include:

* The ability to study interventions that cannot be directed toward selected individuals (e.g., a radio show about lifestyle changes) and the ability to control for "contamination" across individuals (e.g., one individual's changing behaviors may influence another individual to do so).<ref name="Edwards-1999">{{Cite journal | vauthors = Edwards SJ, Braunholtz DA, Lilford RJ, Stevens AJ | title = Ethical issues in the design and conduct of cluster randomised controlled trials | journal = BMJ | volume = 318 | issue = 7195 | pages = 1407–9 | year = 1999 | url= | pmid = 10334756 | pmc=1115783 | doi=10.1136/bmj.318.7195.1407}}</ref> 
* Reduced cost in running a [[Survey (human research)|survey]]. For example, when wanting to survey households, it could often be cheaper to choose street blocks and survey all the houses there in order to reduce the cost of traveling for the people conducting the survey.<ref>[https://www.coursera.org/learn/sampling-methods Sampling People, Networks and Records] coursers course (worth finding a better reference)</ref>{{Better source needed|date=May 2025}}
* Sometimes due to data availability, it is only possible to do [[cluster sampling]]. For example, if wanting to survey households, it may be that there is no census list of houses (due to privacy restrictions of the [[List of national and international statistical services|Bureau of Statistics]] of the country). However, there may be a public record of street blocks and their addresses, and these can be used for creating the [[sampling frame]].

==Disadvantages==
Disadvantages compared with individually randomised controlled trials include greater complexity in design and analysis, and a requirement for more participants to obtain the same [[statistical power]].<ref name="Campbell-2004"/>  Use of this type of trial also means that the experiences of individuals within the same group are likely similar, leading to correlated results. This correlation is measured by the [[intraclass correlation]], also known as the intracluster correlation. Though this correlation is a known component of cluster-randomised controlled trials, a large proportion of the trials fail to account for it. Failing to control for intraclass correlation negatively affects both the [[Power of a test|statistical power]] and the incidence of [[Type_I_and_type_II_errors#Type_I_error|Type I errors]] of an analysis.<ref name="Murray"/>
